groups.title: Solutions to overtourism
groups.instruction: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

parts.context: A lecturer explains overtourism and possible solutions.

transcript.text: Good afternoon. Today I want to talk about a problem that affects many popular destinations: overtourism. It describes a situation where too many visitors damage the quality of life for residents and the experience for tourists.
transcript.speaker: DR LANE

transcript.text: The term became widely used around two thousand and sixteen, as cheap flights and social media made travel easier than ever. Photographs of beautiful places spread quickly, and crowds followed them.
transcript.speaker: DR LANE

transcript.text: Tourism is, of course, extremely important for many local economies. In some places, it provides more than a quarter of all jobs, so the aim of policy is not to stop it but to manage it. That distinction is central to everything I will say today.
transcript.speaker: DR LANE

transcript.text: Venice is the classic example. The historic centre has only about fifty thousand residents, but it receives roughly twenty-five million visitors every year. Many streets are so crowded that local people avoid them.
transcript.speaker: DR LANE

transcript.text: The effects are easy to see. Shops that once served local residents are replaced by souvenir stalls, and families who have lived in the same neighbourhood for generations decide to move out because they can no longer afford the cost of living.
transcript.speaker: DR LANE

transcript.text: Many of these visitors are day-trippers who come off cruise ships, spend a few hours, and spend very little money. Residents complain about noise, crowded streets and rising rents.
transcript.speaker: DR LANE

transcript.text: Another example is Barcelona, where tourist apartments rented through websites have reduced the supply of housing. As a result, prices for local families have gone up sharply.
transcript.speaker: DR LANE

transcript.text: Similar stories can be found in many other places, from islands in the Mediterranean to mountain villages in Asia. The details differ, but the pattern is the same: rapid growth in visitors, rising prices and a feeling among residents that the town no longer belongs to them.
transcript.speaker: DR LANE

transcript.text: Amsterdam has taken action. It banned new hotels in the city centre and introduced a limit on the number of nights apartments can be rented, currently thirty.
transcript.speaker: DR LANE

transcript.text: Not everyone agrees with these restrictions. Hotel owners argue that they reduce income and jobs, and some visitors feel that they are being treated as a problem rather than as guests. Finding a balance is clearly not easy.
transcript.speaker: DR LANE

transcript.text: So what can be done? Firstly, destinations can charge an entry fee. Venice introduced a fee of five euros for day visitors in peak periods, and the money is used to maintain the city.
transcript.speaker: DR LANE

transcript.text: Secondly, tourism can be spread more evenly across the year. Many places now promote the off-season, when the weather is cooler but prices are lower and the atmosphere is more authentic.
transcript.speaker: DR LANE

transcript.text: Thirdly, visitors can be guided to lesser-known areas. Some cities have created smartphone apps that suggest quiet neighbourhoods instead of the famous squares.
transcript.speaker: DR LANE

transcript.text: None of these measures works alone. The most successful destinations combine several of them, and they also consult residents, because a policy that local people support is far more likely to succeed than one that is imposed from above.
transcript.speaker: DR LANE

transcript.text: Finally, travellers themselves have a role. Staying in a local guesthouse, buying from small shops and visiting outside peak hours all help spread the benefits to residents.
transcript.speaker: DR LANE

transcript.text: I'll leave you with a question: is it fair to limit who can visit a city? We'll discuss that next week. Thank you.
transcript.speaker: DR LANE
